title: Intercultural Competence
before: How cultural meaning shapes ordinary DSD conversations, and how to choose a response that fits the person rather than our own default.

turns.text: Intercultural Competence is a course about ordinary moments in DSD work: a renewal conversation, a team meeting, a comment on a proposed service change. In each of them, cultural meaning shapes what people say and what we think they meant. The course asks how those everyday choices affect services and workplace opportunity, both for the people we serve and for the colleagues we work with.

It starts with a service discussion that accepts comments only during the meeting. Someone needs more time, or another way to contribute. Nobody meant to exclude them, but their knowledge may be missed, and if the format keeps repeating, it can narrow whose experience shapes services. I like that the course asks you to choose one change and name what you would check with participants.

The same pattern can happen inside a team. A newcomer is unsure about unwritten expectations and stays quiet, and the silence gets read as lack of interest. If that reading shapes later assignments, an onboarding gap becomes an opportunity gap. So the course keeps returning to a useful question: what evidence would change your first interpretation?

That connects to the difference between intention and impact. A staff member answers for a person because they want to be helpful, and the person loses the chance to explain their own priorities. The intent was kind, but if it becomes routine, the plan may end up reflecting other people’s assumptions rather than what the person actually wants.

Independence is a good example of how meaning varies. For one person it may include close family relationships, while staff may assume it means doing everything alone. That assumption can narrow the options anyone discusses. A community brief can help you prepare better questions, but it cannot tell you what this particular person means. Only the person can explain that.

Then the course compares two familiar ideas. The Golden Rule asks us to offer the care and respect we would want for ourselves. The Platinum Rule asks how the other person wishes to be treated. Our own preferred approach can make information or feedback harder for someone else to use, even when it feels generous from where we stand.

Intercultural competence ties those pieces together: understanding cultural meaning and choosing an appropriate response. You will also meet the Intercultural Development Continuum, which describes orientations from Denial through Adaptation. The course is clear that it is there to examine practice approaches and what they might overlook. It is not for labeling people, and nothing you answer here establishes anyone’s IDI result.

The practice situations are private, and you do not need to share personal or case information. You will think through a person who sets aside a translated renewal notice while family offers to answer every question, a new employee who contributes mostly in writing, and a familiar community partner whose comment is treated as the whole community’s view.

There are shorter situations as well: a caller speaking loudly about a service delay, a person who once raised a discrimination concern, and a family who calls an offered option “welfare.” Each one asks how to describe what actually happened without guessing intent, and how to keep an early judgment from traveling into records and later decisions.

What I appreciate is that the course does not treat one adjustment as the finish line. You try something supported by what you learn, then ask whether it helped or only changed the interaction. If the same barrier keeps returning, that may point to a routine that needs attention, not just a single conversation that went differently.

So as you begin, think of one service or workplace routine you know well, such as a meeting format, a notice, or the way new staff are introduced. Whose voice or opportunity might it affect if it keeps running the way it does now? Keep that example nearby, because the course will give you questions to trace it and to decide what you would check afterward.

guidance.title: Meaning and response together
guidance.text: Intercultural competence is less about knowing facts about every culture and more about connecting two things: what an exchange means to the other person, and a response that fits. Begin by asking whose expectations built the routine in front of you and how it affects who can take part. Then try a change, and look for signs that people could participate more fully, not only that the exchange felt different.

guidance.title: Before you decide what it meant
guidance.text: Think about the short situations you just worked through: the renewal notice set aside, the loud call, the earlier complaint, and the declined offer. Which one feels closest to a moment in your own work? What did you notice first, and what did you assume about it? If you met that moment again tomorrow, what open question would you ask before deciding what it meant?
